UNE COM · OMS-1 Psychiatry Block · Lecture Notes

Sexual, Somatoform & Dissociative Disorders

Ryan Smith, DO, PhD — "Somatoform Disorders, Factitious Disorder and Malingering," "Dissociative Disorders," and "Sexual Disorders" 2026
Topics3 lecture parts, 1 combined handout
Core SplitUnconscious (somatoform) vs. conscious (factitious/malingering) symptom production
Boards FactMalingering = external gain; Factitious = sick role (internal/primary gain)
High-YieldLa belle indifférence · DID alters · Paraphilia vs. paraphilic disorder
Yield check: This handout stitches together three shorter lecture segments that all share a theme: symptoms without a clear organic explanation — whether that's a physical complaint (somatoform spectrum), a break in the continuity of identity/memory/reality (dissociative spectrum), or a pattern of sexual functioning or interest (sexual disorders). The single highest-yield organizing question across the whole handout is: is production of the symptom conscious or unconscious — and if conscious, is the goal external gain (malingering) or the sick role itself (factitious disorder)?
Section 01 · Part I

Overview: Psychosomatic Theory & DSM-5's Two Categories

The relationship between psychological events and physical health has long been recognized — the precise mechanism has just never been fully clear.

Early Psychodynamic View

ModelSpecific psychological conflicts in childhood cause specific physical conditions in adulthood — hypertension, peptic ulcer, colitis, asthma, migraine, arthritis were all once framed this way.

Modern View

ModelDe-emphasizes any one-to-one conflict-to-disease mapping; focuses instead on the general relationship between psychological stress and physical symptoms broadly.

Two DSM-5 Categories Built on This Relationship

Psychological factors affecting other medical conditions — psychological factors are temporally associated with the initiation or exacerbation of a real, diagnosable medical condition. Classic example: stress worsening GERD.
Somatoform disorders — mental disorders characterized by physical symptoms that suggest, but are not fully explained by, a general medical condition.

The full DSM-5 "Somatic Symptom & Related Disorders" chapter — this handout focuses on the first 4

The Master Organizing Question ⭐ HY

🧠
Every disorder in this chapter splits along one line: is the symptom unconsciously or consciously produced? That single distinction is the fastest way to sort any vignette in this section.
Unconsciously-ProducedConsciously-Produced
DisordersSomatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety disorder, conversion disorderMalingering, factitious disorder
IntentSymptoms and illness motivation are NOT intentionally producedIntentional production or feigning of symptoms
EpidemiologyMore common in womenVaries by specific disorder (Section 04)
Section 02 · Part I

Unconsciously-Produced: Somatic Symptom, Illness Anxiety & Conversion Disorders

Somatic Symptom Disorder

PictureA variety of complaints across one or more organ systems, lasting months to years, associated with excessive and persistent thoughts about the symptoms. May genuinely co-occur with real medical conditions — the psychological preoccupation is disproportionate to whatever organic pathology is (or isn't) present.
VideoNone available for this one per the handout.

Illness Anxiety Disorder (Hypochondriasis)

PicturePreoccupation with and fear of having a serious medical illness, despite medical evidence and reassurance to the contrary. Unlike somatic symptom disorder, the somatic symptoms themselves may be minimal or absent — it's the fear/preoccupation that's the disorder.
▶ Illness anxiety disorder case 🔒 UNE

Conversion Disorder

Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder
PictureSudden loss of sensory or motor function — paralysis, blindness, mutism — often following an acute stressor. Classically more common in females, young adults, and adolescents.
Signature findingLa belle indifférence — the patient is aware of the symptom but shows a striking, disproportionate lack of concern about it.
▶ Conversion disorder case 🔒 UNE
📌
La belle indifférence, translated: "the beautiful indifference." It's the single most quotable, most testable finding in this section — a patient who has just gone functionally blind or paralyzed, but who seems almost unbothered by it. Note it's a classic association, not a required or universal criterion for conversion disorder — plenty of real patients with conversion disorder are appropriately distressed.
Section 03 · Part I

Diagnostic Clues to Somatoform Disorders

How these patients actually show up in clinic, organized the way a vignette will present them:

Presenting complaints — dramatic, multiple, and peculiar complaints; extreme anxiety or a profound lack of anxiety about minor medical problems; medical complaints presenting alongside clear psychological issues.
History — often vague; complex medical problems abound; multiple past workups with inconclusive findings; a trail of past or current treatment by many different physicians.
Mental status exam — may show anxiety, or a peculiar indifference to significant medical complaints (echoing la belle indifférence from Section 02).
Physical exam/labs — often inconsistent with the medical complaints, or don't map onto any known physiological mechanism.
🩺
Reading this pattern as a vignette: a patient with a thick chart, a long list of specialists already seen, normal or inconsistent workups, and a symptom picture that doesn't fit any single organic disease process is the classic setup for a somatoform-spectrum diagnosis. The specific disorder then comes down to what kind of complaint dominates (diffuse multi-system complaints → somatic symptom disorder; fear of illness despite reassurance → illness anxiety disorder; a discrete neurological deficit → conversion disorder).
Section 04 · Part I

Consciously-Produced: Malingering & Factitious Disorder ⭐ HY

Both involve the intentional production or feigning of physical or psychological symptoms. Both frequently produce anger and exasperation in doctors and staff — which can itself lead to suboptimal care and missed real diagnoses ("The Boy Who Cried Wolf" problem). Some patients will genuinely harm themselves in the process of faking a condition.

Malingering

Not itself a psychiatric diagnosis — a V-code / behavior
MotivationDriven by external incentives — the classic "secondary gain": financial compensation, disability payments, avoiding work, avoiding legal consequences, obtaining drugs.
PatternPoor compliance with treatment, follow-up, or diagnostic testing (since genuine treatment isn't actually the goal). The complaints cease once the gain is achieved — a key differentiator from factitious disorder.
▶ Malingering case 🔒 UNE

Factitious Disorder

A true psychiatric diagnosis
MotivationDriven by a desire to assume the sick role and receive medical attention itself — this is primary gain, not an external reward.
Munchausen syndromeThe chronic form, predominantly physical signs/symptoms — a history of multiple hospital stays and a striking willingness to undergo invasive procedures.
Munchausen syndrome by proxyIllness is caused in a child or elderly dependent by their caregiver, so the caregiver can occupy the sick role by proxy. This is a form of child/elder abuse and must be reported to authorities.
▶ "Rebecca" — factitious disorder case 🔒 UNE

Diagnostic Clues

Presenting complaints — dramatic, peculiar, and changing medical complaints, often with an identifiable environmental incentive for illness lurking in the background.
History — vague/complex medical problems; guardedness about revealing past complaints or assessments; multiple inconclusive past workups; treatment by many physicians; a history of signing out of hospitals against medical advice (AMA); noncompliance with treatment/diagnostics.
Mental status exam — anxiety, peculiar indifference to significant complaints, and (a real tell) extreme familiarity with medical terminology or procedures — often beyond what a layperson would know.
Physical exam/labs — inconsistent with known physiological mechanisms; possible signs of multiple prior surgical procedures.
Section 05 · Part I

Putting It All Together: Comparison Table & Flowsheet ⭐ HY

The master comparison — gain type, deliberateness, psychiatric-disorder status, and willingness to undergo procedures

GainDeliberate?Psychiatric Disorder?Agrees to Procedures?
MalingeringExternalYesNoNo
Factitious DisorderSick roleYesYesYes
Somatization (somatic symptom disorder)None (unconscious)NoNoNo
📌
The willingness-to-undergo-procedures row is an underrated tell: a malingerer avoids invasive workups (there's nothing to find, and procedures don't serve their external goal); a factitious-disorder patient often welcomes invasive procedures, since undergoing them is the sick role they're seeking.

Flowsheet: From Unexplained Symptoms to Diagnosis

Unexplained symptoms → is there a conscious attempt to deceive? No → somatoform disorder. Yes → is the chief goal psychological (1° gain) or external (2° gain)? Psychological → factitious disorder. External → malingering.

🧠
One clean decision tree, memorized: (1) Is there a conscious attempt to deceive? If no → somatoform disorder (somatic symptom, illness anxiety, or conversion, depending on presentation). If yes → (2) is the goal psychological/internal (wanting to be sick, cared for, the center of medical attention) or external (money, work avoidance, drugs, legal advantage)? Internal/psychological → factitious disorder. External → malingering.
Section 06 · Part II

Dissociative Disorders: DSM-5 Overview

Dissociative disorders share a common thread: a disruption in the normally integrated functions of consciousness, memory, identity, or perception. DSM-5 recognizes 4 core diagnoses (plus "other specified" and "unspecified" catch-alls):

300.14 Dissociative identity disorder · 300.12 Dissociative amnesia (specify: 300.13 with dissociative fugue) · 300.6 Depersonalization/derealization disorder · plus other specified/unspecified

Dissociative identity disorder — disruption of identity into 2+ distinct personality states (Section 07)
Dissociative amnesia (± fugue) — inability to recall important autobiographical information, sometimes with purposeful travel/wandering (Section 08)
Depersonalization/derealization disorder — persistent or recurrent detachment from self or surroundings, with reality testing intact (Section 09)
Section 07 · Part II

Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID) ⭐ HY

Previously known as multiple personality disorder.

Full DSM-5 criteria A–E

CriterionRequirement
ADisruption of identity with ≥2 distinct personality states (may be described in some cultures as possession); marked discontinuity in sense of self/agency, with related alterations in affect, behavior, consciousness, memory, perception, cognition, and/or sensory-motor functioning — observable by others or reported by the individual
BRecurrent gaps in recall of everyday events, important personal information, and/or traumatic events, inconsistent with ordinary forgetting
CClinically significant distress or impairment
DNot a normal part of a broadly accepted cultural/religious practice (in children: not better explained by imaginary playmates or fantasy play)
ENot attributable to a substance or another medical condition (e.g., complex partial seizures)

Etiology

DID's proposed etiology

💡
DID is thought to result from severe trauma during early childhood — usually extreme, repetitive physical, sexual, or emotional abuse. The dissociation is theorized as a protective/coping mechanism that allows the developing mind to compartmentalize unbearable experience.

How the Alters Relate to Each Other ⭐ HY

Three classic relationship patterns between alternate identities (Murray, 1994)

Pattern 1 — mutually aware of each other
Pattern 2 — mutually unaware of each other
Pattern 3 — one is aware of the other, but the awareness is not reciprocated

In its simplest form, two personalities alternate, each unaware of the other. A more complex pattern involves two or more dominant personalities plus one or more subordinate ones.

DID vs. PTSD, Chronic/Severe (With Dissociative Traits) ⭐ HY board-relevant controversy

⚖️
There is genuine, ongoing debate in the field about whether DID is best understood as its own distinct entity, or whether many presentations currently labeled DID are better conceptualized as a severe, chronic form of PTSD with dissociative features. Both share the trauma etiology and dissociative symptomatology; the distinction matters for how clinicians and researchers frame treatment and prognosis. This is worth knowing exists as a controversy, even without a settled "right answer."

Treatment options — psychotherapy/cognitive therapy is the backbone; hypnosis, medication, ECT, and adjunctive treatments play supporting roles

Conceptualizing DID on a Spectrum

🎙️
Dr. Smith's own note on the chart below: "This chart is not completely accurate, but is a good way to conceptualize it." Treat it as a teaching heuristic, not a literal diagnostic scale.

A conceptual severity spectrum, plus a 13-step general treatment framework (trust/therapeutic alliance → diagnosis → communication with personalities → contracting therapy → safety assessment → history-gathering → working through issues of each personality → special procedures → interpersonality communication → resolution/integration → new coping skills → social networking → solidifying skills → follow-up)

Section 08 · Part II

Dissociative Amnesia & Fugue State

Full DSM-5 criteria A–D, plus coding notes and the dissociative fugue specifier

CriterionRequirement
AInability to recall important autobiographical information, usually traumatic/stressful, inconsistent with ordinary forgetting
BClinically significant distress or impairment
CNot attributable to a substance or a neurological/medical condition (e.g., partial complex seizures, transient global amnesia, TBI)
DNot better explained by DID, PTSD, acute stress disorder, somatic symptom disorder, or a neurocognitive disorder

Plain-language summary of the same criteria

🧠
Three sub-patterns of dissociative amnesia: localized/selective amnesia for a specific event or events, or generalized amnesia for identity and life history. The amnesia may be continuous from a traumatic event to the present, or cover a person's entire life, and can last hours to years. Information isn't permanently lost — it simply can't be retrieved during the episode.
📌
Dissociative fugue — a specifier, not a separate diagnosis (coded 300.13/F44.1 vs. 300.12/F44.0 without it). Defined as apparently purposeful travel or bewildered wandering associated with amnesia for identity or other important autobiographical information — the person doesn't just forget who they are, they may leave home and turn up somewhere else entirely, sometimes having taken on a new identity.

Statistics, Causes & Treatment

Both conditions usually begin in adulthood, show rapid onset and dissipation, and occur more often in females

Cause — little is definitively known, but trauma and stress appear heavily involved
Treatment — most people with dissociative amnesia/fugue recover spontaneously, without treatment, and most eventually remember what they'd forgotten
Section 09 · Part II

Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder ⭐ HY

Full DSM-5 criteria A–E

DepersonalizationDerealization
TargetAltered perception of oneselfAltered perception of the external environment
ExperienceUnreality, detachment, or being an outside observer of one's own thoughts, feelings, sensations, body, or actions — perceptual alterations, distorted sense of time, unreal/absent self, emotional or physical numbingThe world (people, objects) is experienced as unreal, dreamlike, foggy, lifeless, or visually distorted — vision distorted so objects appear larger or smaller than they really are, or people seem to be strangers, robots, or dreamlike/foggy figures
📌
The single most important criterion to remember: Criterion B — reality testing remains intact throughout the episode. The patient knows their perception is distorted; they aren't psychotic, and this is what separates depersonalization/derealization disorder from a primary psychotic disorder despite the surface-level strangeness of the experience.

Depersonalization as "the sensation that mind and body have separated" — often described by patients as an out-of-body experience

Side-by-side: depersonalization = altered perception of oneself; derealization = altered perception of the external world

💡
Like the other dissociative disorders, depersonalization/derealization occurs far more frequently following a prolonged period of stress or a traumatic event — the same underlying trauma-and-stress etiology runs through this entire section (Sections 07–09).
Section 10 · Part III

Freud & Psychosexual Development Theory

The historical entry point for how sexual disorders were originally conceptualized — largely superseded as a clinical framework, but still worth knowing as background, and it still explains some of the older diagnostic terminology you'll encounter (e.g., "anal-retentive" from Section 12 of the personality disorders unit traces directly back to this model).

The 5 psychosexual stages, their erogenous zones, and the theorized consequences of getting "fixated" at each one

StageAge RangeErogenous ZoneFixation Consequences
OralBirth – 1 yearMouthAggressive: chewing gum, biting pencil ends. Passive: smoking, overeating, oral sexual practices.
Anal1–3 yearsBowel & bladderRetentive: obsessively organized or excessively neat. Expulsive: reckless, careless, defiant, disorganized.
Phallic3–6 yearsGenitaliaOedipus complex (boys) / Electra complex (girls); theorized site of superego development.
Latency6 – pubertyDormant sexual feelingsSexual unfulfillment.
GenitalPuberty – deathSexual interests matureFrigidity, impotence, unsatisfactory relationships.
💭
Freud's original theory proposed that various paraphilias and sexual aversions arose from fixation at a particular psychosexual stage — a historically influential idea, though it isn't the operative explanatory model in modern DSM-5 nosology (Section 12), which classifies paraphilic disorders descriptively rather than by presumed developmental cause.
Section 11 · Part III

Sexual Dysfunctions

DSM-5 splits sexual disorders into two buckets: sexual dysfunctions and paraphilias

📜
Why the DSM-5 list looks the way it does: earlier DSM editions organized sexual dysfunctions around Masters and Johnson's four-stage human sexual response cycle (excitement → plateau → orgasm → resolution). That linear model drew significant criticism for oversimplifying real sexual response. DSM-5's response: it dropped the cycle-based organization and simply lists sexual dysfunction diagnoses alphabetically, since no single agreed-upon model of sexual response currently exists.

The current DSM-5 list, split by sex

MaleFemale
Hypoactive sexual desire disorderSexual interest/arousal disorder
Erectile disorderOrgasmic disorder
Premature (early) ejaculationGenito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder
Delayed ejaculation—
Substance/medication-induced sexual dysfunctionSubstance/medication-induced sexual dysfunction
🩺
Scope note: per the handout, the sexual dysfunctions themselves are covered in depth in the reproductive system block, so they get lighter treatment here. One clinically useful question worth carrying forward: how do you distinguish psychogenic from physiologic erectile dysfunction? The classic bedside/historical clue is the presence or absence of nocturnal or early-morning erections — physiologic (organic) ED typically abolishes these as well as ED with a partner, while psychogenic ED classically spares nocturnal/morning tumescence, since the physiologic machinery is intact and it's the waking psychological context that's inhibiting function.
Section 12 · Part III

Paraphilias ⭐ HY

DSM-5's working definition of paraphilia

📖
DSM-5 definition: a paraphilia denotes any intense and persistent sexual interest other than sexual interest in genital stimulation or preparatory fondling with phenotypically normal, consenting adult human partners.

Paraphilia vs. Paraphilic Disorder — The Critical Distinction ⭐ HY

The distinction that DSM-5 deliberately built into the nomenclature

📌
A paraphilic disorder is a paraphilia that causes distress or impairment to the individual, or harm to others. This distinction matters clinically and diagnostically: you would ascertain a paraphilia based on actions and self-report (e.g., a self-reported sexual attraction to amputees or inanimate objects), but you only diagnose a paraphilic disorder once distress, impairment, or harm to others is actually present. Having an atypical sexual interest is not, by itself, a psychiatric diagnosis under DSM-5's framework — the disorder label requires the added element of distress/impairment/harm.

DSM-5 Paraphilic Disorders

The 8 named paraphilic disorders in DSM-5, with their object of sexual attraction/interest

DSM-5 DiagnosisObject of Sexual Attraction
Fetishistic disorderAn inanimate object
Transvestic disorderCross-dressing
Pedohebephilic disorderChildren
Voyeuristic disorderWatching unsuspecting others undress or have sex
Exhibitionistic disorderExposing one's genitals to an unwilling stranger
Frotteuristic disorderSexual touching of an unsuspecting person
Sexual sadism disorderInflicting pain
Sexual masochism disorderReceiving pain
⚖️
Legal note relevant to several of these: voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, and frotteuristic disorders by definition involve a non-consenting other party — as does any sexual contact with a child. These aren't simply private preferences; they involve actual or potential harm to others, which is part of why they clear the "paraphilic disorder" bar regardless of the individual's own reported distress level.

Paraphilias "Not Otherwise Specified" (NOS)

A longer list of less-common named paraphilias that don't have their own dedicated DSM-5 diagnostic category — coded as "other specified paraphilic disorder" when they cause distress, impairment, or harm

💡
Asphyxiophilia — a newer area of discussion in DSM-5, referring to sexual arousal linked to self-induced oxygen restriction; it's clinically significant partly because of the real risk of accidental death, distinct from its classification questions as a paraphilia per se.
Section 13 · Part III

Treatment of Paraphilias

Who ends up in treatment, and the main treatment modalities used

Who Seeks Treatment

Court-ordered treatment — individuals who have engaged in illegal acts involving a paraphilia
Self-distress — individuals internally motivated to change
Distress due to sexual dysfunction — individuals who can't become aroused or achieve orgasm without the paraphilic activity, and seek help for that functional impairment

Types of Treatment

Incorporation therapy — the paraphilic behavior is decreased or modified to more acceptable levels, without aiming for complete abolition
Psychotherapy — talk therapy
Orgasmic reconditioning — a conditioning-based therapy where the person is trained to become aroused and achieve orgasm in a socially acceptable context that bears no resemblance to the paraphilic stimulus
Drug therapy — used when a brain/glandular chemical imbalance is contributing to unwanted, inappropriate sexual behavior; medications may help alter the production or effects of those chemicals
💊
Pharmacologic mechanism, in practice: the drug therapy referenced here is typically androgen-lowering treatment (e.g., antiandrogens, GnRH agonists) or high-dose SSRIs — both work by reducing the intensity/frequency of sexual drive and intrusive sexual thoughts, rather than "curing" the underlying paraphilic interest itself. This is most relevant in court-ordered or high-risk treatment settings where reducing the frequency of harmful behavior is the primary clinical/legal goal.
Section 14 · Part III

Medical Conditions to Rule Out

The same principle that runs through every unit in this course applies here too: before attributing a change in sexual behavior to a primary psychiatric or paraphilic process, rule out an organic cause — particularly for new-onset hypersexuality, which can be a presenting sign of real neurological or endocrine disease.

Medical conditions associated with hypersexual symptoms, and their proposed pathophysiology

Medical ConditionPathophysiology
Brain injuryDamage to the temporal/frontal lobes (areas that regulate libido)
Klüver-Bucy syndromeDamage to temporal/frontal lobes
Kleine-Levin syndromeHypothalamic or circadian dysfunction
Neurological conditions (Huntington disease, Alzheimer disease)Adrenal disease (adrenal tumor, functioning pancreatic endocrine tumor)
Endocrine conditionsAberrations in adrenocortical production
Drug side effectsOveractivity of the dopaminergic mesolimbic pathway (e.g., dopaminergic agonists)
📌
Board-relevant trigger phrase: dopaminergic agonists (used for Parkinson's disease and restless leg syndrome) are a well-documented cause of drug-induced hypersexuality and other impulse-control problems (compulsive gambling, shopping) via overactivation of the mesolimbic dopamine pathway — the same reward circuit implicated in addiction. A new hypersexuality complaint in a patient recently started on a dopamine agonist should prompt medication review before a psychiatric workup.
💊
Drug classes referenced in this handout's final page: "Uppers/stimulants" and PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil-class drugs) — both relevant to the pharmacologic side of sexual functioning, though the handout doesn't elaborate further here; PDE-5 inhibitors are covered in depth in the reproductive system block per Section 11's scope note.
Section 15

Practice Questions

Vignette-style questions covering the key discriminators from this handout. Tap an option to check your answer.

Question 1
A 22-year-old woman develops sudden-onset blindness shortly after witnessing a fatal car accident. Neurological exam, imaging, and ophthalmologic workup are all normal. She describes her vision loss matter-of-factly and seems remarkably unconcerned about being unable to see. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Malingering
B. Illness anxiety disorder
C. Conversion disorder
D. Factitious disorder
Answer: C. Sudden loss of a sensory/motor function following an acute stressor, with a normal workup and la belle indifférence — a striking lack of concern about the deficit — is the textbook picture of conversion disorder (Section 02).
Question 2
A 45-year-old man has had 2 years of repeatedly normal endoscopies, imaging, and labs, yet remains convinced he has stomach cancer. He has minimal actual GI symptoms but spends hours daily researching cancer online and is not reassured by his physicians' explanations. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Somatic symptom disorder
B. Illness anxiety disorder
C. Conversion disorder
D. Generalized anxiety disorder
Answer: B. The hallmark here is fear/preoccupation with having a serious illness despite minimal actual symptoms and repeated reassurance — that's illness anxiety disorder (Section 02), distinguished from somatic symptom disorder by how little the actual physical symptom burden is, relative to the psychological preoccupation.
Question 3
A man involved in a pending disability claim repeatedly reports severe, disabling back pain and requests a specific opioid by name. He is observed lifting heavy furniture without difficulty when he believes no one is watching, and all of his complaints resolve entirely once his disability claim is approved. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Malingering
B. Factitious disorder
C. Somatic symptom disorder
D. Conversion disorder
Answer: A. Conscious production of symptoms for a clear external incentive (the disability payment), with complaints ceasing once that gain is achieved — the defining pattern of malingering (Sections 04–05), not factitious disorder (which would persist regardless of external reward, since the goal is the sick role itself).
Question 4
A nurse is admitted multiple times for recurrent, unexplained hypoglycemic episodes. Exogenous insulin syringes are eventually found hidden in her belongings. She expresses eagerness for further testing and invasive procedures, and appears to derive comfort from the medical attention despite the real risk to her health. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Malingering
B. Factitious disorder (Munchausen syndrome)
C. Somatic symptom disorder
D. Illness anxiety disorder
Answer: B. Deliberate self-induced illness (exogenous insulin), a welcoming attitude toward invasive procedures, and no identifiable external incentive — the goal is occupying the sick role itself (primary gain). The chronic pattern of multiple hospitalizations for self-induced physical illness is specifically Munchausen syndrome (Section 04). Extensive medical knowledge (she's a nurse) is also a classic risk factor/diagnostic clue.
Question 5
A mother repeatedly brings her toddler to the ED for unexplained episodes of vomiting and bleeding that only occur while the mother is alone with the child. Staff note the mother seems unusually knowledgeable about the child's IV lines and appears to want the child hospitalized. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
A. Discharge the child home with outpatient follow-up
B. Refer the mother for outpatient psychotherapy and reassess in 6 months
C. Report to child protective services / appropriate authorities
D. Confront the mother directly and ask her to stop
Answer: C. This is Munchausen syndrome by proxy (Section 04) — illness induced in a dependent by a caregiver seeking the sick role by proxy. This is a form of child abuse and must be reported to the appropriate authorities; it is not a situation to manage solely through counseling or direct confrontation.
Question 6
A woman reports recurrently "losing time" — finding herself in unfamiliar places with no memory of how she got there. Her family reports that she sometimes speaks in a markedly different voice and refers to herself by another name. She has a history of severe, repeated childhood abuse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Dissociative amnesia with fugue
B. Dissociative identity disorder
C. Depersonalization/derealization disorder
D. Brief psychotic disorder
Answer: B. Distinct personality states (a different voice, a different name) plus recurrent gaps in recall, on a background of severe early childhood trauma, is the DID picture (Section 07) — distinguished from simple dissociative amnesia by the presence of actual alternate identity states, not just memory gaps alone.
Question 7
A man is found 300 miles from home with no memory of his identity. It's discovered he has been living under a different name for the past two weeks. No substance use or medical cause is identified on workup. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Dissociative identity disorder
B. Dissociative amnesia, with dissociative fugue
C. Depersonalization/derealization disorder
D. Malingering
Answer: B. Apparently purposeful travel (or bewildered wandering) associated with amnesia for identity is the definition of the dissociative fugue specifier (Section 08) — coded alongside dissociative amnesia, not as a stand-alone diagnosis.
Question 8
A patient describes feeling, during panic attacks, as though she is "watching herself from outside her body," and says the world sometimes seems "foggy and unreal." She is clear, however, that she knows these feelings are not literally true. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Brief psychotic disorder
B. Depersonalization/derealization disorder
C. Dissociative identity disorder
D. Schizotypal personality disorder
Answer: B. Out-of-body-type detachment from self (depersonalization) plus a foggy/unreal perception of the environment (derealization), with reality testing intact (she knows it isn't literally true), is exactly Criterion A + B of depersonalization/derealization disorder (Section 09) — intact reality testing is what rules out a primary psychotic process.
Question 9
A man reports a longstanding, exclusive sexual interest in a particular inanimate object. He engages with this interest privately with a consenting partner, reports no personal distress, and has a stable job and relationship. Does he meet DSM-5 criteria for a paraphilic disorder?
A. Yes — any paraphilia by definition qualifies as a disorder
B. No — a paraphilia only becomes a paraphilic disorder when it causes distress or impairment to the individual, or harm to others
C. Yes, because fetishistic interests are always pathological
D. It cannot be determined without a formal psychological test
Answer: B. This is precisely the paraphilia-vs-paraphilic-disorder distinction (Section 12): the interest itself (ascertained by self-report/action) doesn't equal a disorder. Without distress, impairment, or harm to a non-consenting party, DSM-5 criteria for a paraphilic disorder aren't met.
Question 10
A 58-year-old man reports the inability to achieve an erection with his partner over the past 6 months, but reports normal, firm early-morning erections upon waking. What does this pattern most strongly suggest?
A. Physiologic (organic) erectile dysfunction
B. Psychogenic erectile dysfunction
C. Substance/medication-induced sexual dysfunction
D. Hypoactive sexual desire disorder
Answer: B. Preserved nocturnal/early-morning erections indicate the vascular and neurologic machinery for erection is intact (Section 11) — pointing toward a psychological rather than organic cause for the situational (partner-specific) dysfunction. Physiologic ED (A) would typically abolish nocturnal erections as well.
Section 16

Rapid Review Grid

Master split
Unconscious production (somatic symptom, illness anxiety, conversion) vs. conscious production (malingering, factitious).
Somatic symptom disorder
Multi-system complaints, months-years, excessive/persistent thoughts about symptoms.
Illness anxiety disorder
Fear of serious illness despite reassurance; minimal actual symptoms.
Conversion disorder
Sudden sensory/motor loss after a stressor; la belle indifférence; F > M, young.
Malingering
External gain; complaints STOP once gain achieved; avoids invasive workups.
Factitious disorder
Sick role = primary gain; WELCOMES invasive procedures; Munchausen = chronic physical form.
Munchausen by proxy
Illness caused in a child/elder by caregiver; mandatory reporting, = abuse.
DID criteria
≥2 distinct personality states + recurrent amnesia gaps; onset = severe early childhood trauma.
DID alter patterns
Mutually aware / mutually unaware / one aware, not reciprocated.
DID vs. PTSD
Ongoing field debate: is DID distinct, or severe/chronic PTSD with dissociative features?
Dissociative amnesia
Localized/selective vs. generalized; info not permanently lost, just unretrievable.
Dissociative fugue
A SPECIFIER of dissociative amnesia (not separate dx) — purposeful travel/wandering + identity amnesia.
Amnesia/fugue course
Usually adult-onset, rapid onset/resolution, F > M; most recover spontaneously.
Depersonalization
Altered perception of SELF (detachment, out-of-body).
Derealization
Altered perception of ENVIRONMENT (foggy, dreamlike, unreal).
Depersonalization/derealization key
Reality testing INTACT — this is what separates it from psychosis.
Sexual dysfunction classification
DSM-5 lists alphabetically (no agreed sexual-response model) — replaced Masters & Johnson's 4-stage cycle.
Psychogenic vs. physiologic ED
Preserved nocturnal/morning erections → psychogenic. Absent → physiologic.
Paraphilia vs. paraphilic disorder
Paraphilia = atypical interest (ascertained). Disorder = + distress/impairment/harm to others (diagnosed).
8 named paraphilic disorders
Fetishistic, transvestic, pedohebephilic, voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, frotteuristic, sexual sadism, sexual masochism.
Non-consent paraphilias
Voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, frotteuristic — inherently involve a non-consenting party.
Paraphilia treatment
Incorporation therapy, psychotherapy, orgasmic reconditioning, drug therapy (antiandrogens/SSRIs).
Hypersexuality red flags
Brain injury, Klüver-Bucy, Kleine-Levin, dopamine agonists (mesolimbic overactivity) — rule out before assuming psychiatric.

⭐ High-Yield One-Pager

Sexual, Somatoform & Dissociative Disorders — condensed pre-exam summary

The Master Split

  • Unconscious production: somatic symptom, illness anxiety, conversion disorder
  • Conscious production: malingering, factitious disorder
  • Decision tree: conscious deceit? No → somatoform. Yes → goal external (2° gain) = malingering; goal psychological/sick role (1° gain) = factitious

Unconscious Disorders

  • Somatic symptom disorder: multi-system complaints, months-years
  • Illness anxiety disorder: fear of illness despite reassurance, minimal symptoms
  • Conversion disorder: sudden sensory/motor loss + la belle indifférence

Conscious Disorders

  • Malingering: external gain; stops once gain achieved; avoids procedures
  • Factitious disorder: sick role (primary gain); welcomes procedures
  • Munchausen = chronic factitious, physical signs, many hospitalizations
  • Munchausen by proxy = caregiver-induced illness in child/elder = ABUSE, must report

Dissociative Identity Disorder

  • ≥2 distinct personality states + recurrent amnesia gaps
  • Etiology: severe early childhood trauma (physical/sexual/emotional abuse)
  • Alter patterns: mutually aware / mutually unaware / one-way awareness
  • Ongoing debate: distinct entity vs. severe/chronic PTSD with dissociative traits

Amnesia, Fugue & Depersonalization

  • Dissociative amnesia: localized/selective vs. generalized; info not permanently lost
  • Dissociative fugue = SPECIFIER (purposeful travel/wandering + identity amnesia)
  • Most amnesia/fugue resolves spontaneously without treatment
  • Depersonalization = self; Derealization = environment; reality testing INTACT (≠ psychosis)

Sexual Dysfunctions

  • DSM-5 lists alphabetically (dropped Masters & Johnson's 4-stage cycle model)
  • Psychogenic ED: nocturnal/morning erections PRESERVED
  • Physiologic ED: nocturnal erections typically ABSENT too

Paraphilias

  • Paraphilia = atypical sexual interest (ascertained by report/action)
  • Paraphilic DISORDER = paraphilia + distress/impairment/harm to others (diagnosed)
  • 8 named: fetishistic, transvestic, pedohebephilic, voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, frotteuristic, sexual sadism, sexual masochism
  • Voyeuristic/exhibitionistic/frotteuristic inherently involve a non-consenting party

Paraphilia Treatment & Hypersexuality

  • Tx: incorporation therapy, psychotherapy, orgasmic reconditioning, drug therapy (antiandrogens/SSRIs)
  • 4 who seek tx: court-ordered, self-distress, sexual dysfunction, (harm risk)
  • Hypersexuality red flags: brain injury, Klüver-Bucy, Kleine-Levin, dopamine agonists

Quick Differentiators

  • Somatic symptom vs. illness anxiety: real physical complaints dominate vs. fear/preoccupation dominates
  • Malingering vs. factitious: stops after external gain vs. persists regardless (sick role is the goal)
  • Factitious vs. somatic symptom: conscious/deliberate vs. unconscious
  • DID vs. dissociative amnesia: alternate identity states present vs. memory gaps alone
  • Depersonalization/derealization vs. psychosis: reality testing intact vs. impaired
  • Paraphilia vs. paraphilic disorder: interest alone vs. + distress/impairment/harm
  • Psychogenic vs. physiologic ED: nocturnal erections preserved vs. absent
  • OCD vs. OCPD (cross-reference): true obsessions/compulsions + ego-dystonic vs. none + ego-syntonic

Built from Ryan Smith, DO, PhD's "Somatoform Disorders, Factitious Disorder and Malingering," "Dissociative Disorders," and "Sexual Disorders" 2026 — UNE COM OMS-1 Psychiatry Block.
